prompt: Choose an architecture for the product search service using the supplied requirements, traffic measurements, option profiles, and price sheet. Produce the public API contract at `api/openapi.json` and explain the choice and tradeoffs at `docs/decision.md`. Keep the API suitable for deep crawler traversal while meeting every hard limit in the input files. In `docs/decision.md`, include a fenced block whose info string is `decision` and whose JSON has exactly `chosen`, `options`, `limits`, and `monthly_cost_usd`. Set `chosen` to the selected option id, `options` to the option ids considered, and make `limits` map each hard-limit name to an object with numeric `limit` and computed `value` fields. Set `monthly_cost_usd` to the selected option's monthly cost computed from the supplied price data, and make the contract document the bounded request size and continuation fields.

checks.cmd: cp hidden/meta.json meta.json && mkdir -p fixture && cp -r hidden/_pristine/. fixture/ && ln -sfn . solution && node --test hidden/*.test.js

rubric.criterion: The decision explains why the selected design meets the deep-traversal latency target and connects each material input to the recommendation. (not code-checkable: A script can recompute measurements but cannot reliably judge whether the explanation is technically coherent or uses the evidence well.)

The decision fairly compares cost, operational capacity, recovery characteristics, client behavior, and migration implications rather than presenting only the winning numbers. (not code-checkable: The tests can check numeric fields but cannot assess whether the prose presents meaningful tradeoffs or acknowledges the rejected option's strengths.)

The API explanation makes the continuation contract understandable to client authors, including replay behavior, final-page behavior, and the reason the value is opaque. (not code-checkable: Schema checks can find fields and constraints, but they cannot determine whether the accompanying explanation is clear and useful to a human reader.)

verdicts.note: The prompt asks to choose an architecture based on supplied data without naming or hinting a specific method or the answer.
All hard limits are clearly defined in the fixture files with explicit direction (max/min) and numeric values.
The fixture files present both options with their metrics but do not state the answer; analysis is required to determine which meets the latency constraint.

The task requires parsing multiple data files, understanding latency calculations, calculating costs, comparing 6 hard limits, producing a valid OpenAPI spec, and writing a decision.md with specific JSON format.
All required numbers are present in fixture files; no unstated format requirements or impossible constraints.

items.text: States that the offset-sql option cannot be selected because its deep-page latency of 4,200 ms (from the deep_offset_p99 measurement in traffic.csv multiplied by the latency_value of 1 in option-profiles.csv) exceeds the 250 ms p99_search_latency limit.
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: States that the old_staging_p99 value of 120 ms in traffic.csv is superseded and must not be used for the latency calculation, as the production measurement at 60 million items is the authoritative source.
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

items.text: Computes the monthly cost using the peak rate of 1,800 req/s from traffic.csv over 30 days at 24 hours per day, with the cursor-index option's fixed cost, storage, and replica charges, arriving at approximately $7,975.81 USD.
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: Explains that the continuation value (cursor) is opaque to clients, which prevents exposing internal storage keys and allows the service to change its index layout without requiring a client migration.

Notes that cursor-index meets the RPO limit of 60 seconds (with 30 seconds) and RTO limit of 15 minutes (with 10 minutes), while offset-sql also meets these limits (45 seconds RPO, 12 minutes RTO) but fails on latency.
items.source: Google SRE Book, https://sre.google/sre-book/table-of-contents/ (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); idea only

items.text: Documents that the limit parameter is bounded (1-100) and that a final page returns a null or absent next_cursor, enabling clients to detect the end of results without counting total records.

Acknowledges that offset-sql has lower monthly cost and sufficient throughput (2,400 req/s) and capacity (60 million items), making the latency constraint the decisive factor rather than cost or capacity.
items.source: AWS Well-Architected Framework, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html (AWS copyright, idea only); idea only

items.text: Explains that cursor-based pagination avoids the deep-page performance degradation inherent in offset-based approaches because it resumes from a known position rather than scanning and discarding earlier rows.
items.source: SQLite query planner docs, https://www.sqlite.org/queryplanner.html (public domain); idea only

weakAnswers: Selects offset-sql because it has lower monthly cost and meets throughput and capacity requirements, without analyzing deep-page latency.
Uses the old_staging_p99 value of 120 ms to justify selecting offset-sql, ignoring the superseded note and the production measurement.
Computes monthly cost using only the fixed and storage charges without including the request volume or replica charges.
Recommends cursor-index without explaining why offset-sql is inadequate, or without comparing RPO, RTO, and migration trade-offs.
Proposes exposing storage keys or internal offsets in the API contract instead of an opaque continuation token.
